### page_1
Paleomagnetic study of the late Neoproterozoic
Bull Arm and Crown Hill formations
(Musgravetown Group) of eastern Newfoundland:
implications for Avalonia and West Gondwana
paleogeography
1
Sergei A. Pisarevsky, Phil J.A. McCausland, Joseph P. Hodych, Sean J. O ’Brien,
Jennifer A. Tait, and J. Brendan Murphy
Abstract: A paleomagnetic study of subaerial volcanic rocks and associated siltstones of the Ediacaran Bull Arm Formation
in the Avalon Zone of Newfoundland revealed a stable bipolar, hematite-borne primary remanence supported by positive
conglomerate, contact, and fold tests. Mean remanence directions in two distal areas (Bonavista and Argentia) are similar,
indicating a low paleolatitude position of Avalonia at ∼570 Ma. Redbeds of the overlying ∼550 Ma Crown Hill Formation
also carry a primary bipolar hematite-borne remanence with moderate inclination, indicating that Avalonia remained at low
to medium paleolatitudes through the end of the Ediacaran. Combining our results with previously published paleomagnetic
data of Avalonia suggests moderate-scale drift of Avalonia through low southern paleolatitudes through the latter half of the
Ediacaran, providing a paleogeographic context for the development of the first complex metazoan life.
Résumé : Une étude paléomagnétique de roches volcaniques subaériennes et de siltstones associés de la Formation de Bull
Arm (Édiacarien) de la zone Avalon de Terre-Neuve révèle une bipolarité stable, une rémanence primaire dans l ’hématite,
laquelle est supportée par un conglomérat positif, un contact et des études sur les plis. Les directions moyennes de la réma-
nence dans deux secteurs distaux (Bonavista et Argentia) sont semblables, indiquant une basse position paléolatitude d ’Ava-
lonia vers ∼570 Ma. Les lits rouges de la Formation de Crown Hill ( ∼550 Ma) sus-jacente conservent aussi une rémanence
primaire bipolaire dans l ’hématite avec une inclinaison modérée, indiquant qu ’Avalonia est demeuré à des paléolatitudes bas-
ses à moyennes jusqu ’à la fin de l ’Édiacarien. Nos résultats combinés à des données publiées antérieurement sur Avalonia
suggèrent un déplacement à échelle moyenne d ’Avalonia à travers de basses paléolatitudes sud durant la deuxième moitié de
l’Édiacarien, fournissant un contexte paléogéographique pour le développement de la première vie complexe des métazoai-
res.
[Traduit par la Rédaction]
Introduction
The late Neoproterozoic was a time of dramatic paleogeo-
graphic changes. One supercontinent (Rodinia) finally broke
up and another one (Gondwana) began to assemble. Several
oceans (Mozambique, Adamastor, Brazilliano) closed during
the formation of Gondwana as others (Iapetus, Paleo-Asian,
Tornquist) began opening between Laurentia, Baltica, Sibe-
ria, Gondwana and other cratonic blocks. However, the pale-
ogeographic reconstructions for this time remain
controversial (e.g., Dalziel 1997; Cordani et al. 2003; Meert
and Torsvik 2003; Tohver et al. 2006; McCausland et al.
2007, 2011; Li et al. 2008; Pisarevsky et al. 2008).
The main reason for this controversy is the sparsely popu-
lated Neoproterozoic paleomagnetic database (McElhinny

### page_2
and Lock 1996; Pisarevsky 2005). Very few reliable and
well-dated paleopoles are available for the major cratons
through the late Neoproterozoic (see reviews of Collins and
Pisarevsky 2005; McCausland et al. 2007; Pisarevsky et al.
2008). Consequently, these data do not allow unequivocal
global paleogeographic reconstructions for the time interval
between ∼620 and 540 Ma (the Ediacaran Period; Knoll et
al. 2004). There is still a paucity of reliable Ediacaran paleo-
magnetic data from many major cratons, such as West Africa,
Congo, Kalahari, Siberia, Amazonia, and others. There is
also controversy regarding interpretation of Ediacaran paleo-
magnetic data from Laurentia and Baltica (McCausland and
Hodych 1998; Pisarevsky et al. 2000, 2001; Meert and Van
der Voo 2001; Cawood and Pisarevsky 2006; McCausland et
al. 2007, 2011).
Paleomagnetic poles from smaller terranes are rarely used
for global paleogeographic reconstructions. Block rotations,
oroclinal bending, and other regional and local processes oc-
cur during the accretion of small terranes to large continents
and their subsequent transport along plate boundaries (e.g.,
Coney et al. 1980; Abrajevitch et al. 2008). The exact orien-
tations of small blocks at different times during these proc-
esses are, therefore, hard to reconstruct. Consequently, only
the paleolatitudes obtained from paleomagnetic studies of
small terranes are usually applicable as constraints for the pa-
leopositions of paleocontinents.
Although faunal endemism indicates temporary separation
of Avalonia (parts of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Eng-
land, southern UK, and Belgium) from Gondwana in the late
Ediacaran and Early Cambrian (Landing 2005), Avalonia is
usually considered to have been located among the Peri-
Gondwanan terranes that were distributed near the northern
(present coordinates) margin of Gondwana, adjacent to Ama-
zonia and (or) West Africa at ∼600–540 Ma (e.g., Kroner
and Hegner 1998; Friedl et al. 2000; McNamara et al. 2001;
Murphy et al. 2004; Thompson et al. 2007; Nance et al.
2008, 2010; Pisarevsky et al. 2008 and references therein).
Avalonia’s paleogeographic position is particularly important
because regional tectonic studies indicate that it faced an
open ocean from the late Neoproterozoic to the early Paleo-
zoic (Murphy and Nance 1989).
The first paleomagnetic data from West Avalonia were
published more that 50 years ago (Nairn et al. 1959). How-
ever, most published results cannot be considered reliable be-
cause of a lack of convincing evidence for a primary
remanence and (or) poor geochronological control. Only a
few paleomagnetic results pass these modern criteria, as will
be discussed later in the text. In this work, we present a new
paleomagnetic study of mid to late Ediacaran volcanic rocks
and redbeds of the Bonavista and Avalon peninsulas, New-
foundland, and discuss their implications for understanding
the paleogeographic history of Avalonia with respect to
Gondwana at the end of the Neoproterozoic.
Geology and sampling
The Bonavista and Avalon peninsulas (Figs. 1, 2) are parts
of the Avalonian tectonostratigraphic zone of Newfoundland
(Williams 1979), which represents the core portion of West
Avalonia (O ’Brien et al. 1996). Paleomagnetic sampling was
conducted during the summer of 2007 in two localities: (1) in
the northern portion of the Bonavista peninsula in the vicin-
ity of Plate Cove West, Red Cliff and King ’s Cove, and (2)
on the western shore of the Avalon peninsula, near Argentia.
The latter sampling supplements a pilot study conducted by
Jordan (1999), the results of which are also included herein.
Bonavista locality: Bull Arm and Crown Hill formations
Neoproterozoic rocks in the eastern part of the Bonavista
peninsula belong to two Neoproterozoic sedimentary basins:
(1) the eastern St. John ’s basin (Figs. 1D, 2), which includes
the Conception, St John ’s, and Signal Hill (Gibbett Hill For-
mation) groups; and (2) the western Bonavista basin
(Figs. 1A; 2), which includes the Connecting Point and Mus-
gravetown groups (O ’Brien and King 2002; Normore 2010).
The basins are separated by the Spillars Cove – English Har-
bour fault (Fig. 2; Normore 2010). All these strata were
folded and faulted in the Siluro-Devonian during collision of
Avalonia with Laurentia (Dallmeyer et al. 1983; O ’Brien et
al. 1996, O ’Brien and King 2002). Oriented paleomagnetic
samples were collected from two units of the Musgravetown
group: bimodal subaerial volcanic rocks of the Bull Arm For-
mation and younger redbeds of the Crown Hill Formation
(Figs. 1, 2).
The Bull Arm Formation consists mainly of dark vesicular
basalt of volcanic-arc affinity with synvolcanic epidote and
hematite alteration, intercalated with reddish massive rhyo-
lites and subordinate clastic sedimentary rocks (O ’Brien and
King 2002; Normore 2010). The subaerial to marine, typi-
cally bimodal succession can be traced southwards from the
Plate Cove area of the Bonavista peninsula through the type
locality at Bull Arm to the Placentia Bay coast of the Avalon
peninsula (Fig. 1); it also crops out on the western coast of
Bonavista Bay (O ’Brien and Knight 1988; O ’Brien and King
2002). The Bull Arm Formation overlies red conglomerate
(Cannings Cove Formation, Fig. 1A) of the basal Mugrave-
town Group, which in turn lies with pronounced angular dis-
cordance on the 620 –610 Ma turbidites of the Connecting
Point Group (Jenness 1963; Dec et al. 1992; O ’Brien 1993;
Fig. 1). The Bull Arm Formation passes upward into the
Rocky Harbour Formation (Fig. 1A) — a widespread shal-
low-marine clastic succession. In the western part of Bona-
vista Bay, the Bull Arm Formation at its contact with the
overlying Rocky Harbour Formation has been dated at
570
þ5
/C0 3 Ma (U –Pb zircon, O ’Brien et al. 1989), providing a
younger limit to the age of the Bull Arm magmatism in that
part of the Avalon Zone. The sampled Bull Arm Formation
lavas from the Bonavista peninsula (Fig. 2) are correlated on
a regional scale with latter units and are, thus, assumed to be
coeval (within analytical error limits).
The main sampling locality for the Bull Arm Formation
lies along highway roadcuts and adjacent quarries between
Summerville and Plate Cove West, with one other quarry lo-
cation on Highway 230, 6 km to the south of Summerville
(Fig. 2). Along a large cliff-forming roadcut and in hilltop
quarries, successive flows of the Bull Arm Formation are
well exposed, dipping moderately to steeply eastwards. In
these sites, we were able to establish a stratigraphic order
within which to interpret the paleomagnetic results. Paleohor-
izontal for some sites was not easy to determine, given the
massive appearance of some flows and only occasional oc-
currence of stratified siltstone. We have applied tilt correction

### page_5
locally where possible, but in some cases have extrapolated
paleohorizontal over tens of metres of stratigraphic section.
Separate cooling units were sampled by recognizing litholog-
ical breaks across siltstone units, alternation between mafic
and felsic flows or the occurrence of ferruginous oxidized
flow tops. In all, 11 separate flows from the Bull Arm For-
mation were sampled in the Bonavista locality.
The overlying Rocky Harbour Formation contains con-
glomerates with mafic and felsic cobbles derived from the
Bull Arm Formation. A large (2 m × 2 m × 1 m) boulder of
conglomerate was sampled next to the Bull Arm sample sites
in the Plate Cove area, to perform a paleomagnetic conglom-
erate test (Graham 1949) of the underlying Bull Arm Forma-
tion.
The Crown Hill redbeds conformably and gradationally
overlie the Rocky Harbour Formation (Fig. 1A) and outcrop
in the northern part of the western horn of the Bonavista
peninsula (Fig. 2). We collected red siltstones to mudstones
from gently northeast-dipping beds at shoreline exposures in
the Duntara area and in three roadcut outcrops along the
Duntara – King’s Cove Highway (sites C15 –C19; Fig. 2).
Red conglomerate of the Crown Hill Formation exposed
near Red Cliff contains mafic and felsic volcanic pebbles of
the Bull Arm Formation (Fig. 2); these were sampled for a
second, regional conglomerate test (site BA13). The Crown
Hill redbeds are disconformably overlain by Lower Cambrian
red and green shales and minor limestones of the Bonavista
Formation, exposed in the core of an open syncline at Keels
that plunges gently to the north (Fig. 2). Penetrative deforma-
tion is pervasive in the core of the syncline, but it is repre-
sented only by widely spaced, subvertical cleavage planes in
the Crown Hill Formation redbeds at Duntara, east of the
Duntara fault. Sites C15 –C19 in the Crown Hill redbeds be-
tween Duntara and King ’s Cove do not appear to require
plunge correction as they lie within a structure that is sepa-
rate from the Keels syncline.
The youngest detrital zircons in the Crown Hill Formation
are ∼557 Ma (Pollock et al. 2009). Hence, the age of the
studied redbeds is bracketed between 557 and 542 Ma, the
age of the base of the lower Cambrian. The Crown Hill For-
mation has been correlated with similar latest Neoproterozic
redbeds of the Rencontre Formation (Long Harbour Group),
exposed in the southwestern Avalon Zone (O ’Brien et al.
1990, 1995; O ’Brien and King 2002). These redbeds overlie
rhyolites dated at 551 ± 6 Ma (O ’Brien et al. 1995; Tucker
and McKerrow 1995). This regional correlation is consistent
with the detrital zircon results and makes the depositional age
constraints for Crown Hill slightly tighter: 551 –542 Ma.
Argentia locality: Bull Arm Formation
For regional comparison the Bull Arm Formation volcanic
rocks were also sampled in the Argentia area of the south-
western Avalon peninsula (Fig. 1, 3), which follows up on
the pilot study by Jordan (1999). Here, the age constrains
are less certain — the Bull Arm Formation in Argentia is
thought to be correlative with the Bonavista exposures (e.g.,
ca. 570 Ma), although no geochronological data exist from
this area. Regional tectonism of the western Avalon Zone of
Newfoundland, which includes both Argentia and Bonavista
areas, has been correlated with that of the adjoining Gander
Zone and is the result of the juxtaposition of the zones dur-
ing regional sinistral transpression along the Dover Fault
shear zone (Fig. 1). Deformation and synkinematic magma-
tism along this crustal boundary is coeval with orogen-scale
tectonism and is dated as mid- to late Silurian (Dunning et
al. 1990, Holdsworth 1991, Schofield and D ’Lemos 2000;
O’Brien et al. 1996; van Staal et al. 1998, 2009; Murphy
and Nance 2002).
Ten paleomagnetic sites were collected by oriented block
sampling (Jordan 1999) and with a portable drill (in this
study), from gently west- and east-dipping flows and interca-
lated siltstones on both limbs of an open anticline exposed in
roadcuts along Highway 100 west of Dunville (Fig. 3; King
1988). Paleohorizontal was readily obtained from the interca-
lated siltstones. From regional mapping, the sample sites in
the east limb are approximately at the same stratigraphic level
as those of the west limb (King 1988), allowing for a simple
paleomagnetic fold test (Graham 1949).
Analytical methods
Remanence behaviour was determined by detailed stepwise
thermal demagnetisation ( ≤20 steps, to 600 °C), using a
Magnetic Measurements MMTD1 furnace and the 2G cryo-
genic magnetometer in the University of Edinburgh (Edin-
burgh, Scotland). Stepwise alternating field (AF)
demagnetisation ( ≤20 steps, up to 100 mT) was also applied,
using an AGICO LDA-3A tumbling demagnetiser. Magnetic
mineralogy was investigated from demagnetisation character-
istics and, in selected samples, from measuring the variation
of susceptibility versus temperature (20 –700 °C) using the
AGICO Kappabridge MFK-FA with the CS3 apparatus. Parts
of the collection were studied in the paleomagnetic laborato-
ries of Oxford University (Oxford, UK), Utrecht University
(Utrecht, The Netherlands), The University of Western Aus-
tralia (Perth, Australia), and University of Windsor (Windsor,
Ontario, Canada). The Argentia locality pilot study (Jordan
1999) was undertaken at Memorial University (St. John ’s,
Newfoundland, Canada), with experimental procedures simi-

regional geological elements of Argentia area, Newfoundland.

Paleomagnetic analysis
Bull Arm Formation, Bonavista locality
Petrographic analysis indicates that the mafic flows of the
Bull Arm Formation are variable in grain size and texture.
The finer grained samples contain rare microphenocrysts of
plagioclase and pseudomorphs of clinopyroxene set in a
fine-grained matrix dominated by chlorite and microlites of
plagioclase that display eutaxitic flow textures. Both the phe-
nocrysts and the microlites are extensively saussuritized and
are primarily altered to epidote, chlorite, and minor calcite.
Opaque minerals occur as ( i) abundant, fine ragged grains
homogenously distributed throughout the matrix, ( ii) inhomo-
genously distributed clusters that surround clinopyroxene
pseudomorphs, ( iii) fine needles within altered plagioclase,
and ( iv) in localized fractures that occur at variable angles to
the flow fabric. For each occurrence of opaques, magnetite
exhibits partial to extensive alteration to hematite.
The coarser grained rocks are less altered and contain mi-
crophenocrysts of augite and plagioclase (now albite). The
augite is partially pseudomorphed by chlorite and epidote.
Plagioclase is variably saussuritized. Opaques are dominated
by magnetite, which is partially to extensively altered to hem-
atite. The freshest flows are relatively coarse grained and
contain olivine that, although variably altered, preserves
some relatively fresh grains. Even in these samples, however,
the opaque minerals are predominantly ragged grains that are
homogenously distributed throughout the matrix and are
moderately to extensively altered to hematite.
Magnetic susceptibility vs. temperature experiments on
specimens from the Bull Arm volcanic rocks indicate a pres-
ence of both magnetite and hematite as potential remanence
carriers (Fig. 4). AF demagnetisation was not effective for
the studied rocks — the maximum field of 100 mT was not
enough for proper isolation and removal of the characteristic
remanent magnetization (ChRM), indicating that the rema-
nence contribution from hematite is dominant. Thermal de-
magnetisation of mafic rocks revealed two stable remanence
components with unblocking temperatures of 500 –580
and >630 °C (Fig. 5). The medium temperature component,
carried by magnetite, is rather scattered, with the varying of
site mean a
95 between 16° and 52° (Table 1). In situ site
mean directions weakly cluster with a south, shallow down
direction, best represented by sites BA3 through BA7. The
overall mean direction for the mid temperature component is
characterized by a Fisher ’s precision parameter k < 3, and is
too poorly described to warrant further statistical analysis.
Demagnetisation of rhyolites associated with some sites was
not successful — the isolated remanence component direc-
tions were random and excluded from further analysis.
The high-temperature hematite-borne component in the
mafic rocks is significantly less scattered than the low-tem-
perature component, and it is bipolar (Table 2; Fig. 6). If the
sites from the main sampling locality north of Summerville
are placed in stratigraphic order, then, from the bottom to
the top we have a “normal” (SW downward) interval (sites
BA5 to BA1), then an “inverse” (NE upward) interval (sites
BA8, BA11, and BA10) and again a “normal” interval on the
top (site BA12). This apparently regular magnetostratigraphic
pattern favours a primary nature of the high-temperature
component. The stratigraphic position of the geographically
isolated site BA6 ( “inverse”) with respect to the main section
is not clear.
Most sites exhibit a Fisherian distribution of specimen di-
rections (Fisher 1953). One exception is site BA7, which pro-
duced an elongated distribution and was excluded from
further interpretation (Fig. 7). The mid-temperature and
high-temperature mean directions of site BA2 are consistently
∼90° clockwise rotated with respect to those of adjacent sites
BA1 and BA3 (Tables 1, 2), suggesting that this site has ex-
perienced an unrecognized local block rotation with respect
to the stratigraphy. It is noteworthy that site BA2 was
sampled from a blocky, massive flow that outcropped in a
vertical fissure through a high road cut and has no paleohor-
izontal control.
The nine site-mean directions form two roughly antipodal
groups (Fig. 6 a), but the reversal test of McFadden and
McElhinny (1990) is negative. However, if site BA5 is ex-
cluded because of its 37° difference from the mean direction,
the test becomes positive (Rc, D = 18.2°, D
c = 19.5°;
Fig. 6 b). As this exclusion might be considered as somewhat
biased, we include site BA5 in the overall mean calculation.
In our view, the reason for the reversal test uncertainty is the
paucity of bedding constraints in the Bonavista section. The
stratified sediments associated with the flows are sparingly
exposed, so we were forced to extrapolate their bedding;
note that the flows and bedding dip moderately to steeply to-
wards the northeast in this section, so uncertainty in paleo-
horizontal will be manifested as inclination errors in the
high-temperature mean directions, causing poor statistics and
uncertainty in the reversal test.
Given these circumstances, we interpret the overall tilt-cor-
rected mean direction of declination ( D) = 209.8°, inclination
(I) = 34.7° ( a
95 = 16.8°), based on five “normal” and four
“reversed” site mean directions, to adequately represent the
ancient hematite-borne magnetization in the Bull Arm For-
mation at the Bonavista locality.

### page_8
Conglomerate tests
Three outcrops were used for conglomerate tests (Graham
1949) of the Bull Arm volcanic rocks. We collected pebbles
and cobbles of both mafic and felsic rocks. However, as the
paleomagnetic study of rhyolite flows typically revealed scat-
tered directions, we used only mafic cobbles for the con-
glomerate tests.
The first outcrop (site BA9) is a 2 m × 2 m × 1 m boulder
of conglomerate from the overlying Rocky Harbour Forma-
tion (Fig. 1). Cobbles of up to 15 –20 cm size are represented
by mafic and felsic rocks of the Bull Arm Formation. The
high-temperature hematite-borne component (Fig. 8 a) in the
mafic cobbles produced a random distribution, but with con-
sistency within cobbles (Fig. 9 a). The Rayleigh statistics r =
R/n = 0.312 compared with r
c = 0.7 for five cobbles at 95%
confidence level (Mardia 1972), so this test is positive.
The second outcrop (site BA13) represents pebble con-
glomerates of the even younger Crown Hill Formation near
Red Cliff (Fig. 2), which contain pebbles of the Bull Arm
volcanic rocks in a red siltstone matrix. This is a regional
conglomerate test, applicable to both the Bull Arm volcanic
rocks and the host Crown Hill Formation. The high-temper-
ature component (Fig. 8 b,8 c) in mafic pebbles shows a pro-
pensity for northerly, upwards directions, but nevertheless is
also positive (Fig. 9 b) with r = 0.44 compared with rc =
0.56 for eight pebbles. We note that the conglomeratic red
beds at Red Cliff are strongly cleaved along planes that dip
steeply to the southeast, parallel to the regional fold axial
planes (Fig. 2); it is possible that some pebble mean direc-
tions with slightly lower (ca. 630 °C) unblocking temperature
carry the signal of a partial overprint that is directed in a
north and shallow upwards direction (Fig. 8 c), acquired dur-
ing folding and penetrative deformation. This apparent north,
shallow up overprint direction is antipodal to the in situ mag-
netite-borne south, shallow down direction found in sites
from the Bonavista Bull Arm volcanic rocks (Table 1). How-
ever, most of the pebbles carry a hematite-borne remanence
(Fig. 8 b) apparently without any overprint.
A third test has been carried out with four mafic clasts in a
2 m thick rhyolite flow and associated red mudstone overly-
ing the site BA6 amygdaloidal basalt flow; this test may be
considered to be an intraformational “pseudo-conglomerate”
test, with the clasts having been drawn from the underlying
basalt flow. The distribution of these clast mean high-temper-
ature hematite-borne component (Fig. 8 d) directions appears
to be random between clasts and consistent within clasts
(Fig. 9 c), although four clasts are too few to carry out a stat-
istically significant test. However, the r = 0.302 is rather
small even compared with r
c = 0.7 for n = 5 (Mardia 1972),
so we consider this test as tentatively positive.
Contact test
A 10 m thick basalt flow at site BA5 is underlain by finely
laminated purple siltstone, which we sampled at 15 cm, 2 m,
and 4 m stratigraphic distances below the flow. Figure 9 d
shows the ChRM directions of the BA5 basalt flow and the
siltstones below the contact. The ChRM direction of the
baked sediment at 15 cm is similar to that of the overlying
basalt flow. The direction of the sample taken 2 m below the
flow is only slightly different and possibly also baked by the
flow. The sample taken 4 m below the flow is magnetized
inversely, so the contact test is positive if we assume that
geomagnetic reversal occurred after the deposition of silt-
stone, but before the cooling of the lava flow. However, we
cannot exclude an alternative possibility that the reversal oc-
curred during the deposition of the sediment located from 4
to 2 m from the contact.
Bull Arm Formation, Argentia locality
In the Argentia area, we collected samples from two limbs
of an open north –south-hinging anticline (Fig. 3). We have
included eight unpublished site mean results from Jordan

### page_10
(1999). Sister undemagnetised specimens from the latter
study were analysed in this work and found to provide simi-
lar demagnetisation results, so we combined all specimen de-
magnetisations to augment the original Jordan (1999) pilot
study.
Specimens from the Bull Arm Formation in the Argentia
locality are sampled from basalt flows and siltstones. As in
the Bonavista area, two remanence components were iso-
lated, but in this case the mid-temperature component yields
a more consistent direction that is directed northwards and
down (Fig. 10) showing a negative fold test (maximum
grouping at –20% unfolding). Hence the age of this compo-
nent is probably post-Silurian. The high-temperature compo-
nent is bipolar (Table 2) and pre-folding (Fig. 11, maximum
grouping at 95% unfolding), with a tilt-corrected mean direc-
tion from seven sites of D = 236.2°, I = 41.2° ( a
95 = 11.2°),
including five “inverted” sites.
Crown Hill Formation, Bonavista peninsula
We collected red siltstone and mudstone samples from the
upper part of the Crown Hill Formation in a coastal outcrop
east of Duntara and in three outcrops along the Duntara –
King’s Cove road, which represent stratigraphically lower
levels (Fig. 2). All strata dip gently to the north-northeast.
Thermal demagnetisation of the Crown Hill red beds show
dominance of hematite (Fig. 12). The bipolar ChRM is quite
stable and consistent (Fig. 13; Table 3). The reversal test of
McFadden and McElhinny (1990) is positive (Rc, D = 3.5°,
Dc = 15.3°). Importantly, the stratigraphically higher sites
(C15a, C15b, C17) and the topmost sample of the strati-
graphically lower site C18 have an exclusively “normal”
(northwest, downward) polarity. The samples in the lower
part of the section (the rest of site C18 and sites C19a and
C19b) have “inverse” (southeast, upward) remanence direc-
tions, except for one sample in site C19a. This magnetostrati-
graphic pattern, supported by the positive reversal test, and
the positive regional conglomerate test sampled in the Crown
Hill Formation at Red Cliff (Fig. 9 b), suggests that the
ChRM carried by the Crown Hill Formation is primary. The
tilt-corrected mean direction from six sites in the Crown Hill
red beds is D = 333.8°, I = 42.4° ( a
95 = 14.6°), including
two “inverted” sites (Table 3).
Discussion
Mid-Ediacaran Bull Arm Formation
In this study, we have found that mafic volcanic flows and
associated siltstones of the Bull Arm Formation carry a pri-
mary hematite-borne ChRM, which is indicated by a positive
(Late Silurian – Early Devonian) fold test for the Argentia lo-
cality and by three positive conglomerate tests in the Bona-
vista locality. The Bull Arm Formation at both localities
features reversals that are stratigraphically controlled. We
consider it likely that the ChRM was acquired soon after the
extrusion of these sub-aerial lavas, probably during oxidation
associated with their cooling.
The Bull Arm result obtained from the Bonavista locality
is from flows that are correlated with Bull Arm volcanic
rocks dated at 570
þ5
/C0 3 Ma (U –Pb zircon; O ’Brien et
al.1989), so we ascribe that age to the Bonavista result (Ta-
Table 4). The Bull Arm result from the Argentia locality has
a more uncertain age, being only constrained to be pre-fold-
ing in age, along with its less clear stratigraphic position with
respect to the dated Bull Arm volcanic rocks. The mean re-
manence directions for the Argentia and Bonavista localities
are similar and their circles of confidence overlap (Fig. 14),
Fig. 6. Bull Arm Formation, Bonavista. ( a) Stereoplot of the site
mean directions of ChRM; ( b) NE upward vectors inverted. Projec-
tion and symbols as in Fig. 5.
Fig. 7. Bull Arm Formation, site BA7 — elongated distribution, ex-
cluded from analyses. Projection and symbols as in Fig. 5.

Published by NRC Research Press

### page_11
so we consider them to be of similar mid-Ediacaran age. It
remains possible that the Argentia locality could be strati-
graphically older than the Bonavista locality, but no older
than 610 Ma (Table 4), based on regional stratigraphic rela-
tionships (Jenness 1963; Dec et al. 1992; O ’Brien 1993;
Fig. 1).
Late Ediacaran Crown Hill Formation
The result from the ca. 550 Ma Crown Hill Formation in-
dicates that West Avalonia lay at 24.2°S ± 5.3°S at the close
of the Ediacaran (Table 4). Notably, the mean direction from
the Crown Hill Formation is rotated over 90° clockwise from
the mean directions of both Bonavista and Argentia ca. 570
Ma Bull Arm results, despite the overall similarity of the
NNE–SSW structural trends in Bonavista and western Ava-
lon peninsulas (Fig. 1), implying tectonic rotation of the
whole terrane, or possibly a 570 to 550 Ma large true polar
wander (TPW) event (McCausland et al. 2007), with Avalo-
nia lying near the TPW axis of rotation. The Crown Hill
mean direction is also, however, strikingly dissimilar to any
from the subsequent Paleozoic records in Avalonia (Hodych
and Buchan 1998), except for the ca. 442 Ma Midland Minor
intrusive suite of East Avalonia, which is similarly anoma-
lous and interpreted to possibly represent a rotated block (Vi-
zan et al. 2003).
Paleogeographic implications for Avalonia in the
Ediacaran
Our new data from Bull Arm and Crown Hill Formations
indicate low to medium paleolatitudes for West Avalonia at
∼570 and ∼550 Ma. Based on the results from this study
alone, West Avalonia appears to have resided at low to me-
dium paleolatitudes during the latter part of the Ediacaran,
placing the ca. 565 Ma Ediacaran fauna-bearing strata at Mis-
taken Point and on the Bonavista peninsula (Narbonne and
Gehling 2003; O ’Brien et al. 2006) at <32°S during their
deposition.
We reviewed other published 620 –540 Ma paleomag-
netic results from both East and West Avalonian terranes
in view of more recent geochronological research on rocks
that had been studied paleomagnetically (Tucker and Phar-
aoh 1991; Compston et al. 2002; Schofield et al. 2010).
After filtering out Phanerozoic overprints and data without
proper demagnetization schemes there are six (including
three new results of this study) West Avalonian and five
East Avalonian paleomagnetic results (Table 4; Fig. 15).
Because of the poor Cambrian paleomagnetic database, the
sign of paleomagnetic polarity for Precambrian Avalonia
results is unclear, but we will assume a southern hemi-
sphere polarity, as suggested by most published Ediacaran
paleogeographic reconstructions (e.g., Dalziel 1997; Cor-
dani et al. 2003; Meert and Torsvik 2003; Murphy et al.
2004; Tohver et al. 2006; McCausland et al. 2007; Li et
al. 2008; Pisarevsky et al. 2008).
Fig. 8. Bull Arm Formation, Bonavista. Conglomerate test —
orthogonal plots. ( a) Site BA9, hematite-bearing ChRM; ( b) site
BA13, hematite-bearing ChRM; ( c) site BA13, possibly partly mag-

Published by NRC Research Press

### page_12
The paleomagnetic results for West and East Avalonia to
first order agree with one another, producing similar paleola-
titude estimates where ca. 600 and ca. 570 Ma comparisons
can be made (Fig. 15). This comparison supports the idea
that West and East Avalonia were together throughout the
Ediacaran, as expected from geological considerations (e.g.,
Cocks and Fortey 1982; McKerrow et al. 1992; Murphy et
al. 2004; Nance et al. 2008 and references therein).
The ages are not uniformly distributed, with only one rela-
tively high paleolatitude of 55° ± 8° from the Roxbury For-
mation, New England (Fang et al. 1986) for the time interval
between 593 and 570 Ma. Its imprecise age is constrained by
the 593 Ma youngest detrital zircon in the lower part of the
formation (Thompson et al. 2007) and by the youngest of a
range of zircon dates of the ash bed in the overlying Cam-
bridge Argillite, which is 570 Ma (Thompson and Bowring
2000). The Roxbury result was characterized by Thompson
et al. (2010) as a possible overprint, but it is apparently sup-
ported by a positive conglomerate test for primary remanence,
though without details (Fang et al. 1986). We retain the Rox-
bury result in Table 4 and in Fig. 15 and leave the judgement
to the reader and future studies of the Roxbury Formation.
All other Avalonia paleolatitudes in Table 4 are below 40°.
We should also note that three results from Uriconian
rocks in East Avalonia with ages between 568 and 564 Ma
(entries 8 –10 in Table 4) all indicate low paleolatitude, but
none of these studies provide convincing evidence for pri-
mary or near primary remanence. However, the correspond-
ing paleopoles lie apart from the Phanerozoic European
Apparent Polar Wander Path (McElhinny and McFadden
2000), so a younger overprint seems to be unlikely.
The paleolatitude drift history of Avalonia can be inter-
preted in two ways: if the solitary higher paleolatitude result
from the Roxbury Formation is primary, then Avalonia would
appear to have moved from paleolatitudes of ∼30°S at
∼600 Ma to ∼55°S during the deposition of the Roxbury
Formation, and then back to ∼35°S or lower paleolatitudes
by 570 Ma. Interestingly, the postulated residence of Avalo-
nia at >45°S at some time between 593 and 565 Ma corre-
sponds with the occurrence of glaciogenic sedimentation in
Avalonia, in the Boston area (ca. 590 Ma; Thompson et al.
2007) and at Gaskiers, Newfoundland (584 –582 Ma; Bowr-
ing et al. 2003; Hoffman and Li 2009).
If the result from the Roxbury Formation is not primary or
if the New England portion of Avalonia was not strictly
amalgamated with the rest of Avalonia at that time, then the

### page_13
remaining paleomagnetic results for Avalonia can be inter-
preted to represent relatively minor variation in low to mid
southerly paleolatitudes from ∼600 Ma onwards through the
Ediacaran.
Geodynamic implications from Avalonian paleomagnetic
results
Application of the Avalonian paleomagnetic results to Ed-
iacaran global paleogeography depends on the proximity of
Avalonia to major continents. Most workers agree that the
Avalonian blocks were Peri-Gondwanan terranes and at 600 –
550 Ma were attached or situated close to the (present) north-
ern margin of Amazonia and (or) West Africa (McNamara et
al. 2001; Murphy et al. 2004; Thompson et al. 2007; Nance
et al. 2008, 2010 and references therein). These two major
continents were probably juxtaposed to each other in a Gond-
wanan configuration (Trompette 1994, 1997). Unfortunately,
Ediacaran paleomagnetic data from Amazonia and West
Africa are scarce and controversial, so their paleolatitudes at
∼600–550 Ma are unknown (Tohver et al. 2006). In this sit-
uation, paleomagnetic data from peri-Gondwanan terranes
may provide paleolatitudinal constraints for these West
Gondwanan cratons. We shall follow this hypothesis of the
West African – Amazonian affinity of Avalonia.
Published global paleogeographic reconstructions for 600 –
550 Ma vary considerably (e.g., Grunow et al. 1996; Dalziel
1997; Cordani et al. 2003; Pisarevsky et al. 2008 and referen-
ces therein). The main reason is the Laurentian paleomag-
netic database, which contains two sets of equally reliable
paleopoles indicating either high- or low-latitude position of
Laurentia correspondingly (see a summary of Pisarevsky et
al. 2008 and references therein). If all of the Ediacaran paleo-
poles for Laurentia are primary, an unusually high rate of
plate movement or some contribution of TPW is required
(McCausland et al. 2007; 2011). Consequently, two alterna-
tive sets of reconstructions have been proposed (Murphy et
al. 2004; McCausland et al. 2007; 2011; Pisarevsky et al.
2008).
Another possibility involves the dominant contribution
from a rapid interchange event in the Earth ’s moment of in-
ertia tensor (inertial interchange true polar wander (IITPW);
Kirschvink et al. 1997). The idea has been further developed
(Evans 1998, 2003) and criticized (Meert 1999; Tsai and Ste-
venson 2007). If the IITPW hypothesis is correct, evidence of
similar rapid apparent polar wander (APW) should be present
coevally in the rock records of all continents. Schmidt and
Williams (2010) demonstrated that there is no large shift in
paleolatitude for Australia, although their compilation does
show a relatively large APW for that continent during the Ed-
iacaran.

### page_14
Recently, Abrajevitch and Van der Voo (2010) suggested
that the controversy of Laurentia and Baltica Ediacaran pa-
leopoles could be explained by an alternation of the geomag-
netic dipole axis between a geocentric coaxial and an
equatorial alignment. This is an interesting idea, but it is in
need of further testing. In particular, as for the IITPW, the
geocentric equatorial dipole hypothesis requires similar be-
haviour of paleopoles from other continents.
In general, the low to moderate southerly paleolatitudes of
Avalonia through the Ediacaran (Fig. 15) imply that the adja-
cent Amazonia – West Africa margin of West Gondwana
similarly did not experience much change in paleolatitude,
thus potentially placing a constraint on global geodynamic
models. The result from the Roxbury Formation (Thompson
et al. 2007) is the only relatively high paleolatitude for Edia-
caran Avalonia (Table 4; Fig. 15) and, consequently, for the
“northern” West Gondwana (northern parts of Amazonia and
West Africa in present coordinates). Excluding the Roxbury
Formation result, the Avalonia paleolatitude distribution sup-
ports a “low-latitude” Laurentia model for the global late
Neoproterozoic paleogeography (Pisarevsky et al. 2008), be-
cause the “high-latitude” Laurentia model requires near-polar
position of this area in mid-Ediacaran time, assuming that
Laurentia and West Gondwana were closely associated
throughout the Ediacaran.
570–550 Ma Avalonia – West Gondwana relations
The mid- and late Ediacaran paleomagnetic results from
Avalonia may be compared with results of similar age from
West Gondwana, if Amazonia and West Africa are taken to
have essentially joined the other elements of West Gondwana
by ca. 630 Ma (Trompette 1997; Cordani et al. 2009). We

### page_16
note, however, that the assembly of West Gondwana by some
interpretations did not take place until the Cambrian (Trin-
dade et al. 2006; Tohver et al. 2010).
The mid-Ediacaran, paleomagnetic database for other West
Gondwanan cratons is also poor. Most results are poorly
dated and their primary remanence is not proven. Moreover,
some of these results are from metamorphic belts, and it thus
is not clear if the corresponding terranes already were ac-
creted on the cratonic margins. However, the SA2 pole in
Rio de la Plata craton (Sanchez-Bettucci and Rapalini 2002;
579 Ma Ar/Ar cooling age from Oyhantçabal et al. 2007)
probably can be used for at least paleolatitudinal constraint.
The expected paleolatitude position of West Avalonia as pro-
vided by the Bull Arm Formation result (Table 4) likely lies

### page_17
within the shaded region of Fig. 16 a, between 8°S and 32°S
along the join between the Amazonian and West African
margins of West Gondwana.
In the late Ediacaran (Fig. 16 b), the ca. 550 (± 50) Ma
Los Barrientos siltstones (Rapalini 2006) and the 547 Ma Si-
nyai metadolerite dykes (Meert and Van der Voo 1996) are
taken to represent West Gondwana. The coeval Crown Hill
Formation paleolatitude is plotted as the shaded region be-
tween 18°S and 30°S along the West African margin of
Gondwana.
The shift in West Avalonia ’s cratonic affinity along the
West Africa stems mainly from the apparent southwards shift
of West Gondwana between 570 and 550 Ma. The relative
motion between Avalonia and the Amazonia – West Africa
margin is represented schematically in Fig. 16 b as a dextral
transcurrent motion of about 1000 km along the margin.
These results are broadly consistent with models in which
Avalonian magmatism is terminated between 600 and 540
Ma by the generation of a San Andreas-style transform fault
(Murphy et al. 2000) and with detrital zircon data from Edia-
caran aged clastic rocks which indicate a shift from Amazo-
nian to West African provenance in the Ediacaran (Gutiérrez-
Alonso et al. 2005).
Conclusions
1. Paleomagnetic study of the ∼570 Ma Bull Arm volcanics
in Bonavista and Argentia localities of the Avalon Zone,
Newfoundland reveal a consistent bipolar ChRM, carried
by hematite, that is likely primary, as shown by several
positive field tests and by apparent magnetostratigraphic
pattern in the studied section. Paleomagnetic directions
are slightly different in Bonavista and Argentia, which
may because of to slight structural differences between
the two localities, or possibly age difference between the
studied rocks. A less stable magnetite-borne component
in the Argentia locality postdates Silurian folding.
2. The paleomagnetic study of the ∼550 Ma Crown Hill red
beds in the northern part of the Bonavista peninsula re-
veal a stable bipolar hematite borne ChRM supported by
positive reversal test and by a magnetostratigraphic pat-
tern in the studied section.
3. These results suggest a low-latitude position of Avalonia
in the mid- to late Ediacaran, during the period when
complex Ediacaran fauna became established in West
Avalonia.
4. Ediacaran paleolatitudes of Avalonia indicate only moder-
ate-scale drift of this terrane and suggest that the Amazo-
nia – West Africa portion of Gondwana underwent little
drift during this time, assuming Avalonia maintained a re-
latively fixed relationship with those cratons.
5. Alternatively, a ∼1000 km dextral motion of Avalonia
with respect to Amazonia – West Africa can be inferred
from the comparison of Avalonia paleolatitudes with the
position of West Gondwana at ∼570 and ∼550 Ma, as-
suming West Gondwana was assembled prior to 570 Ma.
